claim: Obesity has always been considered a significant risk factor in osteoarthritis (OA) progression.
source: Obesity has always been considered a significant risk factor in osteoarthritis (OA) progression, but the underlying mechanism of obesity-related inflammation in OA synovitis remains unclear.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific consensus and citations in the introduction.

claim: Obese OA patients showed a more pronounced synovitis and enhanced macrophage infiltration in synovial tissue compared to non-obese OA patients.
source: The present study revealed that obese OA patients and Apoe−/− mice showed a more pronounced synovitis and enhanced macrophage infiltration in synovial tissue, accompanied by dominant M1 macrophage polarization.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pathology analysis of human and mouse tissues shown in Figure 1.

claim: Apoe−/− mice showed a more pronounced synovitis and enhanced macrophage infiltration in synovial tissue.
source: The present study revealed that obese OA patients and Apoe−/− mice showed a more pronounced synovitis and enhanced macrophage infiltration in synovial tissue, accompanied by dominant M1 macrophage polarization.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mouse model studies shown in Figure 2.

claim: Obese OA patients and Apoe−/− mice showed dominant M1 macrophage polarization in synovial tissue.
source: The present study revealed that obese OA patients and Apoe−/− mice showed a more pronounced synovitis and enhanced macrophage infiltration in synovial tissue, accompanied by dominant M1 macrophage polarization.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing increased iNOS-positive M1 macrophages in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Obese OA mice had more severe cartilage destruction than OA mice in the control group.
source: Obese OA mice had a more severe cartilage destruction and increased levels of synovial apoptotic cells (ACs) than OA mice in the control group.
evidence: This claim is supported by OARSI scoring data and histological analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Obese OA mice had increased levels of synovial apoptotic cells compared to control OA mice.
source: Obese OA mice had a more severe cartilage destruction and increased levels of synovial apoptotic cells (ACs) than OA mice in the control group.
evidence: This claim is supported by TUNEL and caspase-3 staining data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Enhanced M1-polarized macrophages in obese synovium decreased GAS6 secretion.
source: Enhanced M1-polarized macrophages in obese synovium decreased growth arrest-specific 6 (GAS6) secretion, resulting in impaired macrophage efferocytosis in synovial ACs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and ELISA data showing reduced GAS6 in obese OA tissues and LPS-treated macrophages in Figure 3.

claim: Decreased GAS6 secretion by M1 macrophages resulted in impaired macrophage efferocytosis of synovial apoptotic cells.
source: Enhanced M1-polarized macrophages in obese synovium decreased growth arrest-specific 6 (GAS6) secretion, resulting in impaired macrophage efferocytosis in synovial ACs.
evidence: This claim is supported by efferocytosis assay data showing reduced phagocytic capacity in Figure 4.

claim: Intracellular contents released by accumulated apoptotic cells trigger an immune response and lead to release of inflammatory factors TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6.
source: Intracellular contents released by accumulated ACs further triggered an immune response and lead to a release of inflammatory factors, such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, which induce chondrocyte homeostasis dysfunction in obese OA patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data showing increased inflammatory cytokines in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inflammatory factors TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 induce chondrocyte homeostasis dysfunction in obese OA patients.
source: Intracellular contents released by accumulated ACs further triggered an immune response and lead to a release of inflammatory factors, such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, which induce chondrocyte homeostasis dysfunction in obese OA patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data showing increased MMP13, p16, and p21 in chondrocytes after AC stimulation in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intra-articular injection of GAS6 restored the phagocytic capacity of macrophages.
source: Intra-articular injection of GAS6 restored the phagocytic capacity of macrophages, reduced the accumulation of local ACs, and decreased the levels of TUNEL and Caspase-3 positive cells, preserving cartilage thickness and preventing the progression of obesity-associated OA.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo intervention data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Intra-articular injection of GAS6 reduced the accumulation of local apoptotic cells.
source: Intra-articular injection of GAS6 restored the phagocytic capacity of macrophages, reduced the accumulation of local ACs, and decreased the levels of TUNEL and Caspase-3 positive cells, preserving cartilage thickness and preventing the progression of obesity-associated OA.
evidence: This claim is supported by TUNEL and caspase-3 staining data in Figure 5C, D.

claim: Intra-articular injection of GAS6 decreased the levels of TUNEL and Caspase-3 positive cells.
source: Intra-articular injection of GAS6 restored the phagocytic capacity of macrophages, reduced the accumulation of local ACs, and decreased the levels of TUNEL and Caspase-3 positive cells, preserving cartilage thickness and preventing the progression of obesity-associated OA.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantification data in Figure 5D.

claim: Intra-articular injection of GAS6 preserved cartilage thickness.
source: Intra-articular injection of GAS6 restored the phagocytic capacity of macrophages, reduced the accumulation of local ACs, and decreased the levels of TUNEL and Caspase-3 positive cells, preserving cartilage thickness and preventing the progression of obesity-associated OA.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis and OARSI scoring in Figure 5A, B.

claim: Intra-articular injection of GAS6 prevented the progression of obesity-associated OA.
source: Intra-articular injection of GAS6 restored the phagocytic capacity of macrophages, reduced the accumulation of local ACs, and decreased the levels of TUNEL and Caspase-3 positive cells, preserving cartilage thickness and preventing the progression of obesity-associated OA.
evidence: This claim is supported by comprehensive histological and scoring data in Figure 5.

claim: Targeting macrophage-associated efferocytosis is a potential therapeutic strategy for obesity-associated OA.
source: Therefore, targeting macrophage-associated efferocytosis or intra-articular injection of GAS6 is a potential therapeutic strategy for obesity-associated OA.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Intra-articular injection of GAS6 is a potential therapeutic strategy for obesity-associated OA.
source: Therefore, targeting macrophage-associated efferocytosis or intra-articular injection of GAS6 is a potential therapeutic strategy for obesity-associated OA.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the therapeutic efficacy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The risk of knee OA was five times higher in obese patients than in healthy individuals.
source: A meta-analysis of joint replacements in obese patients in 2010 has shown that the risk of knee OA was five times higher in obese patients than in healthy individuals (Clement and Deehan, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis study.

claim: Being overweight doubled the proportion of joint replacement treatments required later in life.
source: At the same time, being 'overweight' (i.e., obesity) doubled the proportion of joint replacement treatments required later in life (Franklin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: By 2025, the global incidence of obesity will reach 18% in men and 21% in women.
source: It is estimated that by 2025, the global incidence of obesity will reach 18% in men and 21% in women (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an epidemiological projection study.

claim: Obesity affects OA by changing certain mechanical factors.
source: It was initially believed that obesity affects OA by changing certain mechanical factors.
evidence: This represents a historical scientific belief mentioned in the introduction.

claim: The progression of OA continues in non-weight-bearing areas even after the line of force is corrected.
source: However, the progression of OA continues in non-weight-bearing areas, even after the line of the force is corrected (Yusuf et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Obesity-related mechanical factors cannot be justified in the development of OA in non-weight-bearing joints such as the hands.
source: Moreover, these obesity-related mechanical factors cannot be justified in the development of OA in non-weight-bearing joints such as the hands (Pottie et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Obese OA patients are often associated with severe chronic synovitis.
source: Clinical data have confirmed that obese OA patients are often associated with severe chronic synovitis, which plays an essential role in the pathogenesis and progression of OA (Sellam and Berenbaum, 2010; Mathiessen and Conaghan, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Synovitis plays an essential role in the pathogenesis and progression of OA.
source: Clinical data have confirmed that obese OA patients are often associated with severe chronic synovitis, which plays an essential role in the pathogenesis and progression of OA (Sellam and Berenbaum, 2010; Mathiessen and Conaghan, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Synovial macrophage polarization is significantly correlated with synovitis in OA progression.
source: Our previous findings have indicated that synovial macrophage polarization is significantly correlated with synovitis in OA progression (Koski et al., 2006; Daghestani et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies including the authors' own work.

claim: When synovitis occurs, macrophages are stimulated by various cytokines and consequently release inflammatory mediators.
source: When synovitis occurs, macrophages are stimulated by various cytokines and consequently release inflammatory mediators (Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Excess energy caused by obesity leads to changes in various cell functions, including angiogenesis and inflammatory cell infiltration.
source: At the same time, excess energy caused by obesity leads to changes in various cell functions, including angiogenesis and inflammatory cell infiltration (Collins et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: GAS6 is a secreted glycoprotein widely expressed throughout the body.
source: GAS6 is a secreted glycoprotein widely expressed throughout the body.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about GAS6.

claim: GAS6 plays a vital role in bridging phosphatidylserine on the surface of apoptotic cells with its receptors Tyro3, Axl, and Mer.
source: It is well known for its vital role in bridging phosphatidylserine on the surface of apoptotic cells (ACs) with its receptors Tyro3, Axl, and Mer, triggering the engulfment of ACs in an inflammatory environment (Bellan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and a citation.

claim: GAS6 triggers the engulfment of apoptotic cells in an inflammatory environment.
source: It is well known for its vital role in bridging phosphatidylserine on the surface of apoptotic cells (ACs) with its receptors Tyro3, Axl, and Mer, triggering the engulfment of ACs in an inflammatory environment (Bellan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Macrophage-related phagocytic process is known as 'efferocytosis'.
source: This macrophage-related phagocytic process is also known as 'efferocytosis', which is beneficial for resolving inflammation (Doran et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a definition supported by established scientific knowledge and a citation.

claim: Efferocytosis is beneficial for resolving inflammation.
source: This macrophage-related phagocytic process is also known as 'efferocytosis', which is beneficial for resolving inflammation (Doran et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Impaired efferocytosis weakens the ability to clear apoptotic cells, inducing the release of inflammatory factors and ultimately causing synovitis.
source: Prior studies have shown that impaired efferocytosis weakens the ability to clear ACs, inducing the release of inflammatory factors and ultimately causing synovitis (Nepal et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Synovial tissues were highly hyperplastic in obese OA patients compared to non-obese OA patients.
source: Interestingly, the synovium tended to be hyperplastic in obese patients and reached a maximum in obese OA patients among the four groups (Figure 1A, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data and synovitis scoring shown in Figure 1.

claim: The number of M1 macrophages in the synovial tissue of the OA group increased significantly compared to the control group.
source: As a result, the number of M1 macrophages in the synovial tissue of the OA group increased significantly compared to the control group.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data in Figure 1B, D.

claim: Synovial tissue in obese OA patients was infiltrated with more M1 macrophages than that in non-obese OA patients.
source: Moreover, synovial tissue in obese OA patients was infiltrated with more M1 macrophages than that in non-obese OA patients (Figure 1B, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data in Figure 1B, D.

claim: Apoe−/− mice are considered an ideal model for investigating obesity.
source: The Apoe−/− mouse model was established to further explore the role of obesity in OA development, as it is considered an ideal model for investigating obesity.
evidence: This is a statement about the suitability of the mouse model based on established knowledge.

claim: Feeding high-fat diets to Apoe−/− mice for a short period accelerates the increase in LDL cholesterol levels and induces an inflammatory state.
source: Previous studies have shown that feeding high-fat diets to Apoe−/− mice for a short period accelerate the increase in LDL cholesterol levels and induce an inflammatory state (Tung et al., 2020; Cao et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Apoe−/− mice may be clinically relevant to pathological progression in obese OA patients characterized by elevated plasma LDL cholesterol levels.
source: Apoe−/− mice may be clinically relevant to pathological progression in obese OA patients characterized by elevated plasma LDL cholesterol levels (Gierman et al., 2014; Gierman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Body weight and plasma lipid levels were markedly elevated in Apoe−/− mice after administering a high-fat and high-energy diet.
source: The body weight and plasma lipid levels were markedly elevated in Apoe−/− mice after administering a high-fat and high-energy diet (Tables 2–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Tables 2-4.

claim: There were no significant differences in knee OA OARSI scores between Apoe−/− and C57BL/6 mice 4 weeks post-surgery.
source: There were no significant differences in knee OA OARSI scores between Apoe−/− and C57BL/6 mice 4 weeks post-surgery (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by OARSI scoring data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The OARSI score was significantly elevated in Apoe−/− mice 8 weeks post-surgery.
source: However, the OARSI score was significantly elevated in Apoe−/− mice 8 weeks post-surgery (Figure 2A, B), accompanied by a higher synovitis score and more infiltrated inflammatory cells (Figure 2A, C), indicating that obesity may promote OA development in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by OARSI scoring data in Figure 2A, B.

claim: Apoe−/− OA mice expressed less aggrecan on cartilage than C57BL/6 mice.
source: In addition, Apoe−/− OA mice expressed less aggrecan on cartilage and more MMP13 on cartilage and synovium than C57BL/6 mice (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data in Figure 2D, E.

claim: Apoe−/− OA mice expressed more MMP13 on cartilage and synovium than C57BL/6 mice.
source: In addition, Apoe−/− OA mice expressed less aggrecan on cartilage and more MMP13 on cartilage and synovium than C57BL/6 mice (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical quantification data in Figure 2D, E.

claim: The percentage of M1-like macrophages was increased with OA progression and reached a maximum in obese Apoe−/− OA mice 8 weeks post-surgery.
source: Notably, the percentage of M1-like macrophages was increased with OA progression and reached a maximum in obese Apoe−/− OA mice 8 weeks post-surgery.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data in Figure 2F, G.

claim: The proportion of positive cells for M2-like macrophages in the OA synovium showed no significant change at both 4 and 8 weeks post-surgery.
source: However, the proportion of positive cells for M2-like macrophages in the OA synovium showed no significant change at both 4 and 8 weeks post-surgery (Figure 2F, G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data in Figure 2F, G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: GAS6 was down-regulated in LPS-induced bone marrow-derived macrophages compared to controls.
source: GAS6, a member of the vitamin K-dependent protein family, has been previously found to be down-regulated in Lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) compared to the controls (GSE53986, Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Noubade et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study and data from GSE53986 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: GAS6 is a critical factor regulating cell proliferation and apoptosis by binding to its receptor Axl.
source: GAS6 was investigated as a critical factor regulating cell proliferation and apoptosis by binding to its receptor Axl.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about GAS6 function.

claim: Macrophage release of GAS6 expressed in both human and mouse normal synovial tissues tended to be diminished, especially in obesity-associated OA.
source: Immunofluorescence (IF) staining analysis indicated that macrophage release of GAS6 expressed in both human and mouse normal synovial tissues tended to be diminished, especially in obesity-associated OA (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data in Figure 3A-D.

claim: GAS6 levels in the synovial fluid from obese OA patients were significantly decreased compared to non-obese individuals.
source: Moreover, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) revealed a significant decrease in GAS6 levels in the synovial fluid from obese OA patients than in non-obese individuals (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Polarized M1 macrophages enhanced by LPS showed M1 macrophage-associated reduction of GAS6 and increases in IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α.
source: An in vitro study in polarized M1 macrophages enhanced by LPS confirmed the M1 macrophage-associated reduction of GAS6 and increases in IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α (Figure 3F, G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and RT-PCR data in Figure 3F, G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of Axl-positive cells in the synovium of obese OA patients, obese Apoe−/− OA mice, and control subjects.
source: Interestingly, F4/80-Axl double staining revealed no significant difference in the number of Axl-positive cells in the synovium of obese OA patients, obese Apoe−/− OA mice, and control subjects (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The expression of MER in OA synovial macrophages decreased significantly, especially in obese Apoe−/− OA and obese OA patients.
source: IF staining analysis indicated the expression of MER in OA synovial macrophages decreased significantly, especially in obese Apoe−/− OA and obese OA patients (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of apoptotic cells was increased in synovial tissues with OA progression, which increased significantly in obese Apoe−/− OA and obese OA patients.
source: Immunochemical TUNEL and caspase-3 staining in the present study revealed that the number of ACs was increased in synovial tissues with OA progression, which increased significantly in obese Apoe−/− OA and obese OA patients (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TUNEL and caspase-3 staining quantification data in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Macrophage efferocytosis was impaired in the obesity microenvironment with reduced capacity for clearing fluorescent apoptotic cells in BMDMs from Apoe−/− mice compared to controls.
source: As expected, macrophage efferocytosis was impaired in the obesity microenvironment with reduced capacity for clearing fluorescent ACs in BMDMs from Apoe−/− mice compared to the controls (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by efferocytosis assay data in Figure 4E, F.

claim: Stimulation with GAS6 enhanced the phagocytotic activity of RAW264.7 cells.
source: Moreover, stimulation with GAS6 enhanced the phagocytotic activity of RAW264.7 cells, while inhibition of the Axl receptor by adding R428 diminished this effect (Figure 4H–K), which were further verified in BMDM primary cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by efferocytosis assay data in Figure 4H-K.

claim: Inhibition of the Axl receptor by adding R428 diminished the phagocytotic activity of RAW264.7 cells.
source: Moreover, stimulation with GAS6 enhanced the phagocytotic activity of RAW264.7 cells, while inhibition of the Axl receptor by adding R428 diminished this effect (Figure 4H–K), which were further verified in BMDM primary cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by efferocytosis assay data in Figure 4H-K.

claim: Adding recombinant mouse GAS6 significantly restored the up-regulation of inflammatory factors IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α induced by LPS in RAW264.7 cells.
source: Adding recombinant mouse GAS6 (rmGAS6) significantly restored the up-regulation of inflammatory factors IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α induced by LPS in RAW264.7 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: rmGAS6 had no obvious effect on the polarization of macrophages.
source: Nevertheless, rmGAS6 had no obvious effect on the polarization of macrophages, while R428 up-regulated CD86 and iNOS in BMDMs (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 4G.

claim: R428 up-regulated CD86 and iNOS in BMDMs.
source: Nevertheless, rmGAS6 had no obvious effect on the polarization of macrophages, while R428 up-regulated CD86 and iNOS in BMDMs (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Intra-articular injection of GAS6 significantly delayed synovial inflammation and cartilage destruction compared to vehicle-treated obese OA mice.
source: Interestingly, intra-articular injection of GAS6 significantly delayed synovial inflammation and cartilage destruction compared to vehicle-treated obese OA mice, manifested as lower synovitis and OARSI scores.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological and scoring data in Figure 5A, B.

claim: Inhibition of Axl by R428 in C57BL/6 OA mice promoted synovial hyperplasia and cartilage destruction and enhanced synovitis and OARSI scores.
source: In contrast, inhibition of Axl by R428 in C57BL/6 OA mice promoted synovial hyperplasia and cartilage destruction and enhanced synovitis and OARSI scores (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological and scoring data in Figure 5A, B.

claim: Intra-articular injection of GAS6 recombinant factor decreased the number of apoptotic cells stimulated by synovitis in synovial tissues.
source: Moreover, intra-articular injection of GAS6 recombinant factor decreased the number of ACs stimulated by synovitis in synovial tissues (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TUNEL and caspase-3 staining data in Figure 5C, D.

claim: The expression of MMP13 was increased after adding co-culture supernatant stimulation, together with senescence hallmarks such as p16 and p21, while COL2 was down-regulated after stimulation.
source: The expression of MMP13 was increased after adding co-culture supernatant stimulation, together with senescence hallmarks such as p16 and p21, while COL2 were down-regulated after stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect of supernatant promoting chondrocyte homeostasis dysfunction was partially alleviated when adding apoptotic cells with rmGAS6 to BMDMs.
source: However, the effect of supernatant promoting chondrocyte homeostasis dysfunction was partially alleviated when adding ACs with rmGAS6 to BMDMs, which were diminished by adding R428 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No apparent proteoglycan loss or increase was found in recombinant human GAS6-treated cartilage explants.
source: Nevertheless, no apparent proteoglycan loss or increase was found in recombinant human GAS6 (rhGAS6)-treated cartilage explants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Western blotting showed no significant differences in the expression of COL2, MMP13, p16, and p21 in primary chondrocytes after stimulation with rhGAS6.
source: Moreover, western blotting showed no significant differences in the expression of COL2, MMP13, p16, and p21 in primary chondrocytes after stimulation with rhGAS6 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Figure 5—figure supplement 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The GAS6/Axl axis might alleviate synovial hyperplasia and protect against obesity-associated OA development.
source: Therefore, these data indicated that the GAS6/Axl axis might alleviate synovial hyperplasia and protect against obesity-associated OA development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Obesity stimulates synovial macrophage infiltration and M1 polarization, which suppress the secretion of GAS6.
source: Obesity stimulates synovial macrophage infiltration and M1 polarization, which suppress the secretion of GAS6.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by data from Figures 1-3.

claim: GAS6 binds to the Axl receptor on macrophages.
source: GAS6 binds to the Axl receptor on macrophages, while GAS6/Axl inhibition promotes the accumulation of ACs by decreasing macrophage efferocytosis to induce chondrocyte degradation and aggravate OA development (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about GAS6-Axl interaction.

claim: GAS6/Axl inhibition promotes the accumulation of apoptotic cells by decreasing macrophage efferocytosis to induce chondrocyte degradation and aggravate OA development.
source: GAS6 binds to the Axl receptor on macrophages, while GAS6/Axl inhibition promotes the accumulation of ACs by decreasing macrophage efferocytosis to induce chondrocyte degradation and aggravate OA development (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by data from Figures 4 and 5.

claim: M1-polarized macrophage infiltration in OA synovial tissue of obese patients is increased.
source: The present study revealed for the first time that M1-polarized macrophage infiltration in OA synovial tissue of obese patients is increased, accompanied by markedly down-regulated secretion of GAS6 and impaired macrophage-dependent efferocytosis for cleaning ACs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1.

claim: M1-polarized macrophage infiltration in obese OA patients is accompanied by markedly down-regulated secretion of GAS6.
source: The present study revealed for the first time that M1-polarized macrophage infiltration in OA synovial tissue of obese patients is increased, accompanied by markedly down-regulated secretion of GAS6 and impaired macrophage-dependent efferocytosis for cleaning ACs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and ELISA data in Figure 3.

claim: M1-polarized macrophage infiltration in obese OA patients is accompanied by impaired macrophage-dependent efferocytosis for cleaning apoptotic cells.
source: The present study revealed for the first time that M1-polarized macrophage infiltration in OA synovial tissue of obese patients is increased, accompanied by markedly down-regulated secretion of GAS6 and impaired macrophage-dependent efferocytosis for cleaning ACs.
evidence: This claim is supported by efferocytosis assay data in Figure 4.

claim: Obesity leads to more severe OA manifestations, including cartilage loss, subchondral bone sclerosis, and synovial inflammation.
source: Obesity has always been considered a significant risk factor in the progression of OA (Kulkarni et al., 2016), leading to more severe OA manifestations, including cartilage loss, subchondral bone sclerosis, and synovial inflammation (Wang and He, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Researchers have accepted the role of synovial inflammation in the pathological progression of OA.
source: Researchers have accepted the role of synovial inflammation in the pathological progression of OA (Mathiessen and Conaghan, 2017; Felson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Apoe plays an important role in maintaining the normal levels of cholesterol and triglycerides in serum by transporting lipids in the blood.
source: Apoe plays an important role in maintaining the normal levels of cholesterol and triglycerides in serum by transporting lipids in the blood (Hatters et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Mice lacking Apoe function develop hypercholesterolemia, increased very low-density lipoprotein and decreased high-density lipoprotein, leading chronic inflammation in vascular disease and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.
source: Mice lacking Apoe function develop hypercholesterolemia, increased very low-density lipoprotein and decreased high-density lipoprotein, leading chronic inflammation in vascular disease and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (Liu et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Obese patients and Apoe−/− mice showed more severe cartilage destruction with enhanced OARSI scores.
source: The present study revealed that obese patients and Apoe−/− mice showed a more severe cartilage destruction with enhanced OARSI scores (Glasson et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by OARSI scoring data in Figure 2 and a citation to the OARSI scoring system.

claim: The lining layer of synovial tissue was more prone to hyperplasia in obese patients.
source: Furthermore, the lining layer of synovial tissue was more prone to hyperplasia.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The number of macrophages increased significantly during the pathological development of OA in obese patients.
source: The number of macrophages increased significantly during the pathological development of OA in obese patients, which manifested as enhanced synovitis scores (Krenn et al., 2006) and increased numbers of F4/80-positive cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The imbalance in M1/M2 macrophage polarization plays a vital role in developing OA inflammation.
source: Recent studies have reported that the imbalance in M1/M2 macrophage polarization plays a vital role in developing OA inflammation (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Macrophages are divided into inflammatory M1 and anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages, though they can be interchanged or transformed into each other during various inflammatory reactions.
source: Classically, macrophages are divided into inflammatory M1 and anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages, though they can be interchanged or transformed into each other during various inflammatory reactions and thus function differently (Funes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Adipose tissue macrophages in obese individuals prefer to express TNF-α, iNOS, and other M1 macrophage markers.
source: Lumeng et al., 2007 have found that adipose tissue macrophages (ATMs) prefer to express TNF-α, iNOS, and other M1 macrophage markers, while ATMs in non-obese individuals highly express M2 macrophage markers.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Adipose tissue macrophages in non-obese individuals highly express M2 macrophage markers.
source: Lumeng et al., 2007 have found that adipose tissue macrophages (ATMs) prefer to express TNF-α, iNOS, and other M1 macrophage markers, while ATMs in non-obese individuals highly express M2 macrophage markers.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The transformation of macrophages is triggered by lipids released by fat cells at the onset of obesity.
source: Some researchers believe that the transformation of macrophages is triggered by lipids released by fat cells at the onset of obesity (Chatterjee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: M1 macrophage infiltration increased in the OA synovial tissue of obese patients and Apoe−/− mice compared to non-obese patients and C57BL/6 mice, accompanied by increased secretion of TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6.
source: We found that M1 macrophage infiltration increased in the OA synovial tissue of obese patients and Apoe−/− mice compared to non-obese patients and C57BL/6 mice, accompanied by increased secretion of TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and RT-PCR data in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: The maintenance of efferocytosis dampens pro-inflammatory cytokine production and initiates inflammation resolution.
source: The maintenance of efferocytosis dampens pro-inflammatory cytokine production and initiates inflammation resolution (Boada-Romero et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: M2 macrophages retain efferocytosis properties, which are crucial for resolving inflammation.
